newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-HOOLIGANISM AGAIN BLIGHTS ITALIAN SOCCER.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-HOOLIGANISM AGAIN BLIGHTS ITALIAN SOCCER.

text.p: For the second consecutive Monday morning, Italian soccer woke up to find itself dealing with the aftermath of fan violence.

Violent episodes in Florence before, during and after a 1-1 draw between Fiorentina and Juventus once again left Italian commentators puzzling over how best to deal with the persistent problem of fan violence.
Fighting in Florence not only left 20 policemen and fans injured but also included an attack on the Juventus team bus by Fiorentina fans close to the stadium.

The disturbances at the traditionally fiercely-contested Fiorentina- Juventus game came just one week after Reggiana fans threw four kilos of metal objects including a bathroom tap at the Parma goal during the Reggiana-Parma derby.
Sunday's violence began when 15 Fiorentina fans launched a lightning attack on the Juventus team bus as it arrived outside the Arturo Franchi stadium before kick-off.
Four windows on one side of the bus were smashed and three players, Alessandro Del Piero, Angelo Peruzzi and Michelangelo Rampulla were lucky to escape uninjured.
Despite the presence of a police escort in front and behind the Juventus bus, all the stone throwing assailants avoided arrest.

Further unrest broke out an hour before kick-off when 1000 Fiorentina fans without tickets attempted to force their way into the ground and came to blows with the 1200 strong police force on security duty.

The violence continued long after the final whistle when Fiorentina fans waiting for the Juventus team to emerge from the dressing rooms threw stones, bottles, bricks and other objects at police, damaging cars and houses in the vicinity of the stadium.
Speaking after the match, Fiorentina President, Senator Vittorio Cecchi Gori condemned the violence.
"What happened outside the stadium before the game was ignoble. Those people are not soccer fans, they're people without flag or homeland.
"I told the Juventus directors that next time I'll have myself tied to the front of the bus even if I'm sure that they'll still throw the stones all the same.
"Those people don't care about Fiorentina, they don't care about anything".
First choice Juventus goalkeeper Peruzzi, one of those hit by flying glass during the attack on the team bus, opted not to play against Fiorentina being replaced by Rampulla.
Later, however, Peruzzi explained that his decision had been made because of a previous rib injury unrelated to the attack on the bus.
"Yeah, we got a bit of a fright. You hear the bangs, you see the windows smash but it didn't last long...and I don't want to give these guys any publicity because in the end, not that much happened.
"It'd be better to have a laugh about how difficult it is to comb your hair with broken glass in it", said Peruzzi afterwards.

Media commentators were less inclined to laugh with Rome daily "La Repubblica" writing: "It's time we started thinking in terms of law and order, as indeed already do many fathers who no longer take their children to soccer matches...
"Just when our soccer is thinking of imitating English soccer's business methods, it wouldn't be a bad idea to try and copy their anti-hooligan measures and their stadium organisation...
"It's important that fans realise that who breaks the law or a window will have to pay for it".
Lawyer Sergio Campana, President of the Italian Players' Association (AIC), repeated a call launched after the Reggiana-Parma game last week.
"I say again that whenever the situation appears to have got out of hand, then the referee has a duty to suspend the match," he said.
